---
title: "Workspace evidence v4"
---

Workspace evidence stores numeric columns as exact binary bytes in immutable
SQLite objects. A completed result selects a fixed manifest, so its arrays and
evidence remain readable after `CircuitRun.close()` and in a fresh process.

## Version domains

One number describes stored evidence: 4. The Workspace envelope, the operation
database, every numeric block and every result manifest declare it.

| Document or store | Version |
|---|---:|
| Plan, Request, ParameterSet and authoring snapshot | Existing per-document versions; canonical bytes unchanged |
| Workspace envelope | Schema 1, with required `evidence_version: 4` |
| Numeric block magic bytes and header, and evidence manifest authority | Evidence 4 |
| Operation database and object references | Internal revision 8; the database metadata also declares evidence 4 |

`identity-v4.schema.json` describes the evidence header, manifests, object
references and Direct chunk summaries. It does not describe sweep chunks or
the evidence of a sweep point; this page does. It does not replace the
authoring document definitions in `identity-v2.schema.json`.

## Binary columns

A numeric object contains eight magic bytes `SCNSIMB4`, an unsigned 64-bit
little-endian header length, a canonical JSON header, and contiguous numeric
column bytes. Each column uses its declared dtype, little-endian representation
and C order. Complex values interleave their real and imaginary components.
Signed zero, NaN payload bits, integer statuses and boolean masks retain their
actual representation.

The closed header binds column ordinals, record paths, dtype, shape, dimension
order, units where declared, offsets and byte lengths. Its context binds the
record's execution identities and chunk ordinal. Direct chunks also bind their
terminal and channel order and family units. Other quantity units and physical
axes remain in the enclosing record and selected manifest. The object reference
hash covers the entire framing, header and column payload.

The storage codec replaces only the closed `dtype`/`shape`/`data_hex` array
vocabulary, actual host arrays, and the existing Direct `frequencies_hz`
numerical sequence. Small scalar and identity envelopes retain their canonical
representation. JSON numerical arrays are rejected by the current evidence
reader rather than interpreted as an older storage format.

## Direct chunk summaries

A Direct result stores the S, Y and Z arrays of each chunk in one object and
the equation evidence of the same call in a separately referenced
chunk-summary object. The root index holds the references rather than the
certificate arrays.

The work evidence of a summary is columnar. A work row is one solved frequency
of the chunk. A frequency that the chunk requests more than once shares one
work row, and a work row that several chunks request appears in each of their
summaries. Every work row of a chunk runs the same checked equations, so the
summary holds:

- six work counters, `work_index`, `source_index`, `check_status`,
  `certificate_status`, `check_position` and `certificate_position`, each as
  one 64-bit integer array over the chunk's ordered work rows;
- for each checked equation, its identity (`site`, `role`, `stage` and
  `derivative_order`) once, and each of its fields `status`, `eta`,
  `residual_numerator`, `residual_denominator`, `performed` and `present` as
  one array whose leading axis is the work rows.

The number of columns therefore depends on the checked equations and not on
the chunk size. `status`, `performed` and `present` are stored as binary64
numbers; `eta` and the residual fields keep their floating-point dtype. Slicing
every array at one work row gives that row's certificate values with their
shape and bits unchanged; `work_evidence_rows` in
`workspace/direct_summary.py` returns the rows in that form.

## Sweep points

A parameter sweep stores its points in chunk objects, in declared order. A
chunk holds each point's own arrays and identities. The bodies a point refers
to are separate objects, and the chunk holds only their locators:

| Locator in the stored point | Body it names |
|---|---|
| `evidence_ref` | The evidence of the point |
| `dependency_refs` | The numerical bodies the point depends on, by their content identity |
| `failure.evidence_ref` | The evidence of a failed point's typed failure |

Each body is stored once. Points with identical bodies, such as a repeated
point, name the same object. A continuation record of a point and the
root-anchor baseline of the result are stored the same way. A stored point or
continuation that carries a body instead of its locator is rejected on read.

A point of a Direct sweep, of an operator sweep or of a response-element sweep
carries work evidence: one work row per solved frequency. Stored, the work
evidence is a list of runs. A run is a stretch of consecutive work rows that
ran the same checked equations, and it uses the columnar layout of a Direct
chunk summary:

- the six work counters, each as one 64-bit integer array over the run's rows;
- for each checked equation, its identity once and each of its six fields as
  one array whose leading axis is the rows;
- for rows of the operator and of a response element, their `view_index` and
  `demand`, once.

The rows of one point normally run one frequency function and form one run.
The number of columns therefore depends on the checked equations and not on
the number of frequencies. A point that solved no frequency row stores no run.

Reading a point expands the runs into the per-row records again, in work
order, with every dtype, shape and bit unchanged. `workspace/sweep_evidence.py`
defines both directions: `stored_sweep_evidence` gathers the rows and
`read_sweep_evidence` returns them. A root sweep solves no frequency row; its
points keep their root packet with one array per field, as a single-point root
call does.

## Publication and lifetime

A Direct call keeps its rows in memory while it runs. Its chunks and chunk
summaries are encoded once and written by the final transaction, together with
the manifest, result, completion, attempt state and success selection. A
Direct call that fails or is interrupted leaves no result object and no staging
object in the operation database.

A parameter sweep keeps its rows in memory as well. The frequency rows of the
point being solved are released when that point is complete. A completed point
is held with its work evidence already gathered into runs, and the final
transaction encodes and writes the points once, chunk by chunk. A chunk closes
before the array bytes of its points pass the scratch budget of the execution
policy, 256 MiB by default; a single larger point is its own chunk. A sweep
that fails or is interrupted leaves no result object and no staging object in
the operation database. The memory a sweep holds while it runs grows with its
number of points.

Neither path uses an operation spool. Optimization retains its existing spool
and lazy stage-history lifetime.

Each public Optimization `stage.history` includes its saved starting baseline
before that stage's ordered evaluation occurrences, matching Memory history.
The stage-history body declares `baseline_locator`: an exact stage/model-bound
candidate reference with its original source and batch ancestry, or `null` when
that stage has no separate baseline occurrence. The baseline retains its full
saved values and certificates. Evaluation SQL indexes and optimizer iteration
and evaluation counters are unchanged. Missing or corrupt baseline declarations
fail through the existing evidence-integrity path; readers never substitute the
global comparison baseline or run another solve.

A new object is read back and checked before its write returns. The final
revision-checked transaction publishes the manifest, result, completion,
attempt state and success selection together. Sweep occurrences retain
declared order, repeated points, executed markers and typed failures.

Readers verify reference structure, content hash, framing, exact byte length
and the closed header before decoding. Missing, truncated or corrupted data
fails through the evidence error path. The block codec raises its integrity
and version errors with the stage `evidence_v4`. Reads never repair data or
invoke a solver.

## Opening a Workspace

Opening an existing Workspace first reads its format metadata without creating
a directory, lock file or writable SQLite connection. A Workspace that declares
another evidence version, including version 3 written by 1.0.0a3, raises
`UnsupportedEvidenceVersionError` and requires a new Workspace and
recomputation. The format is checked again under the ordinary lock before
current-format mutation or recovery. There is no migration and no reader for
another version.

The public Sweep, SParameterTrace, Result evidence and resolve interfaces retain
their ownership and ordering. Direct and Operator Results expose readonly same-call evidence, including
each Sweep point and saved resolution. Conditional affine evidence is present
only when that call used it. Public history contains the complete saved stage
baseline and ordered evaluations; iteration/evaluation counters remain separate.
